Field studies of the Snowy sheathbill (Chionis albus) have documented the initial wet weight of newly hatched chicks, which emerges from the egg at approximately 45 grams [Ww0 = approximately 45 grams]. This mass is relatively modest for a charadriiform chick and reflects the trade-off between egg size and the energetic demands of embryonic development in the cold subantarctic environment. Hatchlings are semi-precocial, covered in dense down, and capable of limited mobility within hours of emergence, though they depend entirely on parental brooding for thermal regulation. The neonatal body mass is soon supplemented by intensive feeding of marine invertebrates, predominantly mollusks and crustaceans, which the adults procure from the intertidal zone. Early growth trajectories indicate that body mass increases rapidly during the first two weeks, driven by frequent provisioning visits from both parents. The initial wet weight is thus a critical starting point for understanding the species' post-hatching energy budgets, particularly given the short window of favorable weather in the breeding season.

The wet weight at birth in Chionis albus has been recorded at approximately 32 grams [Wwb = approximately 32 grams], a value supported by measurements from a monitored colony on the Antarctic Peninsula. Hatchlings at this mass are notably small relative to the adult size, indicating a substantial growth phase ahead. This neonatal mass is influenced by the nutritional condition of the laying female, which itself depends on the abundance of intertidal prey during the pre-laying period. Field workers have noted that eggs from females in poorer body condition tend to produce lighter chicks, though the survival prospects of such individuals remain poorly quantified. The 32 grams birth mass contrasts with the much larger adult body mass, underscoring the scale of post-hatching development required before the chick can achieve independence. Comparisons with other sheathbill populations suggest that this value may vary geographically, with birds from more southerly latitudes producing slightly heavier hatchlings on average, possibly as an adaptation to colder incubation conditions.

Under the thermal conditions typical of artificial incubation for several avian species, eggs of the Snowy sheathbill maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after an incubation period of approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days]. This value aligns with data from field nests where internal egg temperatures are regulated by attentive brooding, though natural nests may experience greater thermal fluctuation. The 36 °C incubation temperature represents the optimal thermal environment for embryonic development, as deviations below this threshold can prolong the incubation period or reduce hatching success. Field records indicate that eggs laid early in the season, when ambient temperatures are lower, sometimes exhibit extended incubation durations, though the modal hatching time remains close to 30 days. This developmental period is typical for Charadriiformes of similar body size, placing the species within the expected range for shorebirds and gulls. The hatching event transitions the chick from dependence on yolk reserves to the initiation of exogenous feeding, a critical shift in energy source.

Once hatched, the nestling chick grows rapidly under the sustained metabolic conditions of the breeding adult's body temperature, approximately 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. Achieving sustained flight capability, or fledging, occurs at 55 days after hatching [tx = 55 days after hatching], a developmental milestone that marks the transition to a mobile juvenile stage at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This fledging age is comparable to that of other medium-sized charadriiforms and reflects the time required for full feather development and flight muscle maturation. The post-fledging period is characterized by continued parental provisioning, as the young bird refines its foraging skills before achieving full nutritional independence. Sexual maturity, or puberty, is attained considerably later, at 165 days after hatching [tp = 165 days after hatching], a delay that allows the immature bird to complete somatic growth and acquire sufficient body condition for the demanding reproductive period at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This pubertal age is relatively early for a bird of this size, suggesting a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction over extended somatic development, though the trade-offs involved remain to be fully explored.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Snowy sheathbill, based on extrapolations from related Larus species in the AnAge database, is estimated at 30 years [am = 30 years] under the metabolic conditions typical of active periods at 40.9 °C at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This longevity is within the range observed for many long-lived seabirds, which typically exhibit slow senescence and high adult survival rates. Reflecting the time required to secure a breeding territory and gain foraging proficiency, first reproduction occurs at 1095 days after hatching [tR = 1095 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. Sexual size dimorphism is evident in asymptotic body mass: heavier individuals, likely males, reach approximately 838 grams [Wwi = approximately 838 grams], whereas others average around 735 grams [Wwi = around 735 grams], a difference that likely reflects divergent reproductive roles. Females lay an average of 2.4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.4 eggs per clutch], producing a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], which together yield a modest annual reproductive output. This strategy, combining a small clutch with a long lifespan, is typical of K-selected seabird species that experience high adult survival but low juvenile recruitment.
